questions.question: Which description best reflects osteoarthritis pathophysiology?
choices: Cartilage loss alone with no other tissue involvement
A whole-joint disorder involving cartilage, bone, synovium, muscles, ligaments, and pain processing
A bacterial infection of every painful joint
A condition diagnosed only by MRI
questions.explanation: OA involves the whole joint and pain system. This explains why radiographs and symptoms may not correlate perfectly.

questions.question: A patient with established knee OA has abrupt severe pain, fever, a hot effusion, and cannot bear weight. What is the best next step?
choices: Treat as a routine OA flare
Urgent evaluation for septic arthritis and other acute monoarthritis causes
Inject the joint immediately without assessment
Wait for a routine x-ray next month
questions.explanation: A hot swollen joint with fever and inability to bear weight can represent septic arthritis, a time-sensitive emergency. Chronic OA does not exclude acute infection or crystal arthritis.

questions.question: Which finding is most typical of knee OA?
choices: Pain worse with activity, crepitus, bony enlargement, and brief stiffness
Prolonged fever and severe erythema in every patient
Sudden painless paralysis
Consistent improvement with complete bed rest
questions.explanation: OA commonly produces activity-related pain, crepitus, bony changes, and brief rather than prolonged morning stiffness. Findings vary by patient and joint.

questions.question: Why is immediate MRI not routine for typical clinically diagnosed OA?
choices: MRI cannot see joints
It may identify incidental degeneration and often does not change initial management
It prevents physical therapy from working
OA is always an emergency
questions.explanation: When the clinical pattern is typical, imaging may not change care. MRI can find incidental degenerative findings that do not explain symptoms.

questions.question: Before recommending an oral NSAID for chronic OA pain, which risk review is especially important?
choices: Kidney disease, GI bleeding, cardiovascular disease, blood pressure, antithrombotics, and interactions
Whether the patient prefers heat to ice without reviewing medical risk
Only the severity of crepitus on examination
Only whether radiographs show osteophytes
questions.explanation: NSAIDs can affect renal, gastrointestinal, cardiovascular, blood-pressure, and bleeding risk. Medication and comorbidity review is essential.

questions.question: What is the most useful way to evaluate OA treatment success?
choices: Only repeat x-rays
Function and patient goals such as walking, sleeping, working, and safe self-care
Whether the joint sounds normal
Whether pain is zero within 24 hours
questions.explanation: Function and meaningful goals guide OA care. Structural change may persist even when mobility and quality of life improve.

questions.question: Which intervention is foundational in OA management?
choices: Individualized exercise and self-management support
Long-term bed rest
Routine long-term opioids
Avoiding all movement
questions.explanation: Education, strengthening, aerobic and balance activity, self-management, and context-appropriate weight support are foundational treatments.

questions.question: A patient has knee pain but limited hip internal rotation and groin pain. Why examine the hip?
choices: Hip pathology can refer pain to the knee
Hip examination is unrelated to knee symptoms
It rules out septic arthritis by itself
It determines NSAID dose
questions.explanation: Hip OA or other hip pathology can present as knee pain. Examining the joint above and below prevents localization errors.

questions.question: When is orthopedic referral reasonable for OA?
choices: Only when an x-ray looks severe
When substantial pain and functional limitation persist despite appropriate nonoperative care and the patient wishes to discuss options
For every first episode of mild pain
Instead of physical therapy for all patients
questions.explanation: Referral is based on function, symptom burden, response to nonoperative treatment, alignment or stability, patient goals, and readiness—not radiograph wording alone.

questions.question: Which statement about psychosocial factors in OA is most accurate?
choices: They prove pain is imaginary
Sleep, fear of falling, mood, stress, and access barriers can affect pain-related disability and treatment success
They replace examination for red flags
They make assistive devices unnecessary
questions.explanation: Psychosocial and environmental factors influence function and recovery. Addressing them validates the patient and expands treatment options.
